ops.title: Owned.Run's forced session costs +27% per run — a kern.proc.all scan per Run
ops.description:
Measured 2026-08-01 during the phase-4 supervision lane, on a box with ~2400 processes.

Owned.Run now always spawns into a dedicated session, so a disposable command disposes of its
descendants — without it, a forked grandchild survived a Close that answered a clean drain. The cost
is that every Run pays one `settleSessionSurvivors`, which calls `probeGroupMembers`: a
`sysctl kern.proc.all` plus one `getsid(2)` per process in the table.

    settleSessionSurvivors        29.0 ms/call
    Run(/usr/bin/true)   188 ms -> 238 ms   (+27%)

The scan is O(all processes on the machine), so the cost grows with what else is running, not with
what daemonkit spawned. A consumer running N short commands pays N such scans — and the design
already routes synckit's runCmd/execSSHOnce and captain-hook's runDeploymentTool onto Run.

The named fix: Darwin's `KERN_PROC_SESSION` replaces the whole-table scan with one targeted sysctl
for the session's own members. It was left out of the lane deliberately because it changes the
enumeration semantics `Recover`, `Spawn` and `Adopt` share, so it wants its own pass with those three
re-verified.

Context for whoever picks this up: a spawn already costs ~26 ms dominated by the durable record's
two fsyncs, not by exec — see [[spawn-costs-26ms-dominated-by-durable-fsync]]. Run is not a cheap
primitive and nothing in the API says so.

ops.text: settleSessionSurvivors resolves a session's members without an O(all-processes) scan
Run's per-call cost is measured before and after, at a realistic process count
